places.name: San Onofre nuclear plant
places.text: The San Onofre nuclear power plant, on the beach here, was long known for its two giant round domes, the containment buildings around its reactors. Its last two reactors were shut down in January 2012, after early wear turned up on more than 3,000 tubes in new steam generators, and in 2013 Southern California Edison retired the plant for good. Crews are taking it apart, and removal of the domes was set to begin in 2027, so they may be partly or entirely gone.
places.more: The first reactor here ran from 1968 to 1992, and two larger ones started up in 1983 and 1984. Until 2012 the plant supplied about a fifth of the power for large parts of Southern California. It sits inside the Marine Corps' Camp Pendleton, and it was guarded by a 25-foot wall against tsunamis. By late 2026, 54 of the site's 66 structures had been demolished, and more than 750 million pounds of crushed concrete, steel and debris had left in 3,219 railcars. The used nuclear fuel stays here, sealed in 123 steel canisters inside concrete, until the federal government takes it away, a duty Edison calls decades overdue.
places.spot: Look for two giant round domes by the ocean. Are they still standing?

places.name: San Onofre and Trestles
places.text: San Onofre, Spanish for Saint Onuphrius, a hermit from fourth-century Egypt, is a 3,000-acre state beach on Marine Corps land leased to California, with more than 2.5 million visitors a year. Surfers on redwood boards came here by the 1940s. Its northern surf breaks, called Trestles, are named for a wooden railroad trestle that surfers walked under to reach the beach. Lower Trestles hosted the pro surfing world tour for many years, and Trestles is set to host the 2028 Olympic surfing contests.
places.more: In the early 1900s the land around the old San Onofre train station was Haven's Ranch, where about 150 residents, most of them Hispanic or Japanese American laborers, grew beans, melons and lettuce. During World War II most of the Japanese American workers left or were forced out under President Roosevelt's Executive Order 9066. Two residents, Fred and Kajiro Oyama, were part of Oyama v. California, a 1948 Supreme Court case that began to strike down California's laws barring people of Japanese descent from owning land. The village by San Onofre Creek was torn down in 1960 to make way for this freeway, and Governor Ronald Reagan created the state beach in 1971. At Trestles, a concrete bridge replaced the wooden trestle in 2012. The creek beneath it, San Mateo Creek, made news in 1999, when endangered southern steelhead trout were found in it, the only ones then known south of Malibu Creek.

places.name: Panhe and Los Cristianitos
places.text: Inland of the freeway, in the San Mateo campground area of San Onofre State Beach, is Panhe, the place at the water. It was one of the largest Acjachemen villages, more than 8,000 years old, with perhaps 300 people when the Spanish arrived. It remains a sacred, ceremonial and burial site for the Acjachemen people, who hold a festival there each year to honor their ancestors.
places.more: On July 22, 1769, the Portolá expedition camped near San Mateo Creek. Padre Juan Crespí wrote that two young girls in a nearby village were dying, and the missionaries were allowed to baptize them. A state plaque says Padre Francisco Gómez performed the first Christian baptism in Alta California near a spring up Cristianitos Canyon. Crespí called the place Los Cristianos, and the name later became Cristianitos, the little Christians, the name on the creek, the canyon and the Cristianitos Road exit. In the 2000s a planned six-lane toll road would have passed about 20 feet from the village site. Acjachemen people, environmental groups and surfers fought it, and in 2016 the toll road agency gave up that route.

places.name: Nixon's Western White House
places.text: On the bluff at Cotton's Point stands La Casa Pacifica, the house of peace, which President Richard Nixon bought in 1969. The press nicknamed it the Western White House. Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev and the president of Mexico visited, and after Nixon resigned he retired here to write his memoirs. The road beside the freeway nearby is named Avenida del Presidente, the Avenue of the President.
places.more: The Spanish-style mansion was built in 1926 for Hamilton Cotton, one of San Clemente's founding financiers, who entertained President Franklin Roosevelt there. Nixon's changes, some made for the Secret Service, included a 1,500-foot wall wrapped around much of the nearly six-acre estate, and Pat Nixon brought a magnolia seedling from the tree Andrew Jackson planted at the White House. The famous Frost/Nixon interviews were first planned for the house, but radio signals from a neighboring Coast Guard navigation station interfered with the TV equipment, so they moved to a supporter's home nearby. The Nixons sold the estate in 1980, and it is still a private home.

places.name: Spanish Village by the Sea
places.text: In 1925 Ole Hanson, a former mayor of Seattle, laid out a 2,000-acre town on old rancho land by the ocean and named it after San Clemente Island. He added a clause to the deeds sending every building plan to an architectural review board, to keep roofs of red tile and walls of white. The rule did not last, but the city still calls itself the Spanish Village by the Sea.
places.more: Hanson pictured his town as a clean canvas five miles long and a mile and a half wide. He built the beach club, the community center and the pier, first built in 1928, and lived in a mansion on the bluff now called Casa Romantica. When the Great Depression hit, he lost the house and all his other holdings, and the town's population fell 70 percent, to about 250 people. Casa Romantica is now a city-owned cultural center above the pier. In 1994 Clarence Lobo Elementary opened here, named for Clarence Lobo, chief of the Acjachemen people from 1946 to 1985. It was the first school in California named for an Indigenous leader.
places.spot: Look for red tile roofs on the hillside houses.

places.name: Dana Point and the hides
places.text: West of the freeway on Pacific Coast Highway, Dana Point is named for Richard Henry Dana Jr., who sailed here in 1835 on the brig Pilgrim and wrote about it in Two Years Before the Mast. Cowhides from Mission San Juan Capistrano were brought to the cliffs, and sailors flung them out to the beach below, a job Dana compared to flying a kite without a string.
places.more: Dana called this stretch the only romantic spot on the coast. The Acjachemen village of Toovannga stood near the mouth of San Juan Creek, close to today's harbor. In 1818 the privateer Hipólito Bouchard anchored here during his raid on the mission. Hobie Alter opened what is called the world's first retail surf shop in Dana Point in 1954. The town has held a Festival of Whales since the early 1970s, over two weekends each March, and in 2019 it trademarked the title Dolphin and Whale Watching Capital of the World.

places.name: Mission San Juan Capistrano
places.text: Just west of the freeway, Mission San Juan Capistrano was founded in 1776. Its Great Stone Church took nine years to build and was by all accounts the grandest in California, until an earthquake brought it down during Mass on December 8, 1812, killing about 40 Acjachemen worshipers. Its ruins still stand. The mission is perhaps best known for its cliff swallows, which tradition says come back each year on March 19, Saint Joseph's Day.
places.more: Before the mission, about 550 Acjachemen people lived in this area. By the end of the mission period in 1833, the mission had baptized 4,317 Native people, and 3,158 of them had died. Its Serra Chapel, from 1782, is called the oldest building in California still in use. The swallows spend the winter around Goya, Argentina, fly about 6,000 miles north, and nest under the mission's eaves and arches from spring through fall. A 1939 radio broadcast of their arrival inspired Leon René's hit song When the Swallows Come Back to Capistrano. Few birds came back in the 1990s and 2000s, a decline linked to new development, and from 2009 to 2017 they skipped the mission, until it lured them back with recorded swallow calls and artificial nests.

places.name: Putuidem village
places.text: Just off the freeway, about a mile north of the mission, stood Putuidem, a mother village of the Acjachemen people that gave rise to other villages. Its name means belly or navel. In a story of the village, the chief's daughter Coronne died suddenly and her body became a mound of earth, and the grieving people slept in a pyramid shape called acjachema, which gave the Acjachemen their name.
places.more: When the mission was built beside it in 1776, the village was drained of people to serve the mission. Much of the site now lies under the sports fields and performing arts center of JSerra Catholic High School. Construction began in 2003 despite protests and lawsuits by Acjachemen people and others, who noted that the school was named for the founder of the mission that displaced the village. Burials and sacred objects, including golden eagle and condor bone fragments, had been found around the old village site. In late 2021, after many delays, a park north of the school opened to commemorate the village, a project of the Acjachemen and the city.

places.name: Trabuco Creek's lost gun
places.text: The freeway crosses Arroyo Trabuco here, a 22-mile creek that runs out of the Santa Ana Mountains to meet San Juan Creek beside the mission. Trabuco is Spanish for blunderbuss, a kind of old shotgun. The story goes that in July 1769 a soldier with the Portolá expedition, camped on a bluff above the creek, found his blunderbuss missing. It was never found, and the creek was named for it.
places.more: Acjachemen and Payómkawichum people lived along the creek for some 8,000 years before the Spanish came. In its natural state it had one of the most significant steelhead trout runs in Orange County, and steelhead were sighted in it again in 2003 and 2005. The last California grizzly bear in the Santa Ana Mountains was shot near Trabuco Canyon. The upper canyon became Rancho Trabuco, and much of that land is now O'Neill Regional Park. Under the freeway the creek squeezes through twin culverts, then drops into a small canyon toward San Juan Capistrano.

places.name: Rancho Mission Viejo
places.text: East of San Juan Capistrano, between Ladera Ranch and San Clemente, lies Rancho Mission Viejo, the old mission ranch, still about 23,000 acres. Irish immigrants Richard O'Neill and James Flood bought it after its owner died in 1882, and under O'Neill it became Orange County's largest wheat producer. His descendants still run it as a working ranch, with cattle, orchards and a nature reserve.
places.more: Before the ranch, this land held the Acjachemen village of Piwiva. Don Juan Forster, brother-in-law of Governor Pío Pico, put the ranch together in the 1840s and at one point held about 200,000 acres, making him one of the largest landowners in the state. In the early 1940s the San Diego County part, 123,620 acres, went to the military to expand Camp Pendleton. In 1963 the family and its partners started the Mission Viejo Company and built the 11,000-acre planned community of Mission Viejo on ranch land. A 2004 plan set aside a reserve of nearly 17,000 acres while new villages went up on the rest. The ranch's orange groves have given way to lemons and avocados, and more than 9,000 avocado trees and 63,000 lemon trees are harvested year-round.

places.name: Saddleback
places.text: On clear days, the two-humped mountain east of the freeway is Saddleback. Its higher summit, Santiago Peak, rises 5,689 feet, the highest point in Orange County, and its crown of antennas sends radio signals across much of five counties. The lower summit, Modjeska Peak, less than a mile away, is named for Helena Modjeska, a Polish stage star who lived in a canyon at its foot in her later years.
places.more: The Acjachemen call Santiago Peak Kalawpa. During most winters, snow falls on it at least once. Helena Modjeska is regarded as the greatest actress in the history of Polish theater. In 1876 she, her husband and a group of friends left Poland for California and bought a ranch near Anaheim, but none of the colonists knew how to farm, so she returned to the stage and became known as the leading Shakespearean actress in America. In September 2024 the Airport Fire, named for a model airplane club near where it started in Trabuco Canyon, burned about 24,000 acres and crossed the ridge of Santiago Peak, damaging some of its radio equipment.
places.spot: Look for a mountain with two humps and a dip between them, like a saddle.

places.name: El Toro Y
places.text: This is the El Toro Y, where Interstate 5 and Interstate 405 meet. It is named for the old town of El Toro, Spanish for the bull, which renamed itself Lake Forest in 1991, and for the Marine air station next door. From 1975 to 2002, traffic here more than tripled, to 356,000 vehicles a day, and after a widening finished in 1997 the road here was 26 lanes wide.
places.more: By the early 1990s the Y was one of the most congested interchanges in the world, fed by a housing boom in south Orange County. Voters approved a half-cent sales tax for transportation in 1990, and Caltrans spent $166 million widening it from 1993 to 1997. The jams also led to the parallel San Joaquin Hills and Foothill toll roads. When El Toro became a city, residents fought for months over the new name. People in newer neighborhoods liked Lake Forest, while longtime residents said it erased the town's history for a name about man-made lakes. The forest is man-made too: 400 acres of eucalyptus planted in the early 1900s.

places.name: El Toro Marine air base
places.text: East of the freeway, the Marines flew from El Toro air station from 1942 until it closed in 1999. The Marine Corps paid James Irvine $100,000 for 4,000 acres of his ranch, land that then held the largest lima bean field in North America. Its runways could take the biggest planes in the military, and while the base was open, every president since World War II landed here in Air Force One.
places.more: The base's patch, a flying bull, was designed by Walt Disney Studios in 1944. During the 1960s many Marines left for the Vietnam War from El Toro and came home through it. On the day he resigned in 1974, Richard Nixon flew from Andrews Air Force Base to El Toro. The base's closing set off a long fight over turning it into a big commercial airport. From 1994 to 2001, $80 million in county and city money went to campaigns on both sides, and the airport's opponents won in 2002. About 1,300 acres became the Orange County Great Park, where the Great Park Balloon rises 400 feet above the surrounding land.
places.wiki: Marine Corps Air Station El Toro

places.name: The Irvine Ranch
places.text: The land around here was part of the Irvine Ranch, which once stretched 23 miles from the ocean to the Santa Ana River. James Irvine and his partners began it in 1864 from old Mexican land grants, after a drought killed a rancher's livestock and forced him to sell. By 1918 the ranch grew 60,000 acres of lima beans, and in the 1960s its fields began turning into the planned city of Irvine.
places.more: When Southern Pacific crews laid track across the ranch without permission, Irvine's ranch hands met them with shotguns, and he let the rival Santa Fe railway build through instead. In 1961 the Irvine Company sold 990 acres to the University of California for one dollar, and architect William Pereira planned a city of 50,000 around the new campus, laid out like a necklace with the university as its pendant. Irvine became a city in 1971 and now has more than 300,000 people. The new city took the family's name, and the old farm town of Irvine by the railroad station was renamed East Irvine.

places.name: Jamboree Road
places.text: Jamboree Road is named for a Boy Scout campout. In 1953 the Irvine Company let the National Scout Jamboree use ranch land where Newport Beach's Fashion Island now stands, the first national jamboree held west of the Mississippi. Thousands of tents went up on land reached only by a muddy two-lane trail, which was soon paved and later renamed Jamboree Road.
places.more: Between 45,000 and 50,000 Scouts came, by different counts, and the master of ceremonies, Bob Hope, joked that with boys from so many other countries they were like the United Nations in short pants. The Irvine Company also helped build a road from a stop on the Santa Fe's Los Angeles to San Diego train, the San Diegan, so Scouts could come by rail. One young Scout there, David Sills of Peoria, Illinois, later moved to Irvine and served four terms as its mayor. Today Jamboree Road runs 15.8 miles, from the edge of Balboa Island to the hills of Orange.
places.spot: Look for the green Jamboree Road exit sign.

places.name: Tustin's giant blimp hangar
places.text: South of the freeway stands one of two giant wooden hangars the Navy built during World War II for blimps that patrolled the coast. The surviving south hangar is more than 1,000 feet long and 17 stories tall, one of the largest wooden structures ever built. Its twin, the north hangar, burned in a fire on November 7, 2023.
places.more: The hangars were built of Douglas fir from Oregon, and in 1993 the American Society of Civil Engineers named them a historic civil engineering landmark. In 1951 the base reopened as the country's first air facility built just for helicopters, and Marines flew from it until 1999. The hangars appeared in movies and shows including The Hindenburg, The X-Files, Pearl Harbor and Star Trek. Firefighters let the north hangar burn because its roof could collapse, and crews began tearing down what was left that December. The south hangar is still used to store and service Goodyear blimps, which come back every year for maintenance and inspections.
places.spot: Look between buildings for a huge curved hangar roof in the distance.

places.name: Orange County's orange groves
places.text: In 1936 Orange County grew a sixth of the nation's Valencia oranges, and by 1948 it had 67,263 acres of them, more than five million trees. Then the postwar boom arrived. In 1949 alone, nearly 7,000 acres of orange trees disappeared, and each year more fell as housing tracts spread. By 1985 fewer than 4,000 acres of Valencias were left, mostly on the Irvine Ranch, and twenty years later fewer than 100.
places.more: The first commercial grove of spring-ripening Valencias was planted in 1875 by R. H. Gilman, on land that is now the Cal State Fullerton campus. A tree took about seven years to bear fruit. By 1936 citrus brought in two-thirds of the county's farm income, and in 1919 perhaps a third of the workers in the city of Orange had some job tied to citrus. At their peak in the early 1940s, 45 packing houses were running, and from 1943 to 1964 the Bracero program brought migrant farm workers north. The last packing house, Villa Park Orchards, moved to Ventura County in 2006.

places.name: Santa Ana, the county seat
places.text: West of the freeway, Santa Ana grew on Rancho Santiago de Santa Ana, granted in 1810 to José Antonio Yorba, a sergeant in the Spanish army. His rancho took in the land of today's Santa Ana, Orange, Tustin, Irvine and Costa Mesa. The modern town was founded in 1869 and became the seat of the new Orange County in 1889. In 1877 it offered the Southern Pacific $10,000 and free land to end its new rail line here instead of in Tustin, and won.
places.more: The Tongva name for this area is Hotuuk, and the village of Pajbenga stood beside the river. The hot, dry autumn winds called Santa Anas are named for Santa Ana Canyon, which they seem to blow out of. City boosters disliked the name so much that they spread a false story that it came from a Native American phrase for devil wind, turned into Satanás, Spanish for Satan. Glenn L. Martin started his first airplane company here in 1912, a forerunner of Lockheed Martin. In 1935 Firestone Boulevard opened as the first direct auto road from Los Angeles, and it was later enlarged into this road, the Santa Ana Freeway.

places.name: Santa Ana River
places.text: The wide channel under the freeway here is the Santa Ana River, the largest river entirely within Southern California, running 96 miles from the San Bernardino Mountains to the sea. Soldiers with the Portolá expedition named it Río de Santa Ana in July 1769, probably because they had just celebrated Saint Anne's Day. The city and the mountains took their names from the river.
places.more: The Tongva and Acjachemen name for the river is Wanaawna. In the Great Flood of 1862 it burst its banks and killed 20 to 40 people, and in 1938 it flooded Anaheim and Orange under up to 4 feet of water, killing almost 60 people and wrecking many citrus groves. Prado Dam was built upstream in 1941, and below Anaheim the river mostly runs in a concrete channel. Upstream in Anaheim, nearly all of its dry-season flow is sent into spreading grounds, where it soaks down through sand and gravel to refill the aquifer that supplies about half of the county's tap water.
places.spot: Look for a wide, usually dry river channel passing under the freeway.

places.name: The Crystal Cathedral
places.text: The huge glass building west of the freeway is Christ Cathedral, built as the Crystal Cathedral and finished in 1980. Its 10,000 rectangular panes are mirrored outside and see-through inside, and when it opened it was described as the largest glass building in the world. Despite the name, no crystal glass was used. Since 2019 it has been the cathedral of the Catholic Diocese of Orange.
places.more: Robert and Arvella Schuller started the congregation in 1955 at the Orange Drive-In Theatre, with Robert preaching from the roof of the concession stand while people listened in their cars. The glass is held on with silicone glue to ride out earthquakes, and the building was designed to withstand a magnitude 8.0 quake. Schuller's Hour of Power broadcasts from here regularly reached about 20 million viewers. After his ministry filed for bankruptcy, the Catholic diocese bought the campus in 2012 and renamed the church. Inside is the Hazel Wright Organ, one of the largest musical instruments in the world.
places.spot: Look for a giant building made of mirror-like glass with a tall silver spire.

places.name: Disneyland
places.text: Just southwest of the freeway is Disneyland, built on 160 acres of orange groves and walnut trees, a site picked by researchers Disney hired to forecast where the region's population would grow. Construction began in July 1954, while this freeway, then U.S. 101, was being built just north of the site, and two extra lanes were added for the expected crowds. The park opened one year and one day later, on July 17, 1955.
places.more: Opening day was by invitation only, but about 28,000 people came, roughly half with counterfeit tickets or by climbing the fence. The traffic jam on the Santa Ana Freeway stretched about seven miles. Temperatures reached 100 degrees, fresh asphalt on Main Street turned soft enough to catch high heels, and a plumbers' strike left few drinking fountains. The day became known as Black Sunday. An estimated 70 million people watched the opening on live television, in a country of 165 million.

places.name: Anaheim's German vineyards
places.text: Anaheim was founded in 1857 by 50 German families from San Francisco, who bought some 1,160 acres near the Santa Ana River for 2 dollars an acre to grow grapes. They named it Annaheim, home by the Santa Ana River. Most of them were carpenters and craftsmen who had never made wine, yet for about 25 years the area was the largest wine producer in California.
places.more: Spanish-speaking neighbors called the settlement Campo Alemán, the German Field. The colonists recruited 30 Chinese laborers in San Francisco, and Chinese workers planted hundreds of thousands of vines and dug a 16-mile canal. After the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, anti-Chinese violence and boycotts shrank their community, and by 1935 only one Chinese resident remained. In 1884 a disease struck the vines, and within a year the wine industry was gone. When scientist Newton Pierce studied it in 1892 it was known as Anaheim disease, and today it is called Pierce's disease. Walnuts, lemons and oranges took the vineyards' place.

places.name: Knott's chicken and boysenberries
places.text: About a mile and a half south on Beach Boulevard, Knott's Berry Farm began in 1923 as a roadside berry stand. In the late 1920s Walter Knott helped a federal berry expert hunt for a big berry grown by Rudolph Boysen, and on Boysen's old farm they found a few frail vines in a field choked with weeds. Knott nursed them back to health, sold the big berries at his stand from 1932, and called them boysenberries after their originator.
places.more: In June 1934 Cordelia Knott served eight fried chicken dinners, at 65 cents each, in the family's 20-seat tea room. The dinners drew such crowds that the Knotts built shops and attractions to entertain people waiting for a table, and in 1940 Walter began a replica Ghost Town honoring pioneers like his own grandparents, who came to California by covered wagon in 1868. Rudolph Boysen was Anaheim's first park superintendent. Today the park draws more than 4 million visitors a year, and the restaurant serves more than 1.5 million chicken dinners each year.

places.name: La Mirada's olive ranch
places.text: La Mirada, Spanish for the look, began as the ranch of Andrew McNally, the Chicago printer and mapmaker of Rand McNally. In 1888 he bought more than 2,200 acres for $200,000 and surrounded his home, Windermere Ranch, with olive, orange and lemon groves. He built a plant to press fine olive oil and a railroad station to ship his oil and fruit across the country.
places.more: McNally and his son-in-law, Edwin Neff, sold parcels with a booklet called The Country Gentleman in California. As late as 1946, a Santa Fe railroad guide gave La Mirada's population as 213, among orange, lemon, walnut and olive groves, oil wells and packing houses. Then the land went to developers, and in the early 1950s La Mirada was promoted as the nation's completely planned city. Houses went up so fast that by 1960 the town had grown from about 100 homes to more than 8,000. McNally's home site is now Neff Park.

places.name: Norwalk and Rancho Los Nietos
places.text: In 1784 the Spanish governor gave a former soldier, Manuel Nieto, the use of all the land between the Santa Ana and Los Angeles rivers, from Mission San Gabriel down to the sea. Rancho Los Nietos started at about 300,000 acres, one of the first and largest Spanish land concessions in California. Norwalk, Downey, Buena Park, Anaheim, Whittier and Long Beach all sit on parts of it today.
places.more: The mission padres protested, and the grant was cut nearly in half, but Nieto still kept about 167,000 acres. In 1834 it was split into six smaller ranchos. In 1869 the Sproul brothers from Oregon bought 463 acres here, and when the railroad came in 1873 they deeded it 23 acres on the condition that it build a passenger stop. Three days after the Anaheim Branch Railroad first crossed what was called the North-walk, Gilbert Sproul surveyed a town site, and in 1874 the name was recorded as Norwalk. By 1900 it was a dairy center with some of Southern California's largest sugar beet farms, and many of the dairy farmers who came in the early 1900s were Dutch.

places.name: Santa Fe Springs gusher
places.text: Santa Fe Springs takes its name from mineral springs that Dr. James Fulton turned into a sulfur spa in the 1870s, and that the Santa Fe Railway bought in 1886. In 1921 a well called Union-Bell blew in as a 2,500-barrel gusher and set off an oil rush. Within a year the field was considered one of the richest in petroleum history, and in the 1920s it produced as much as 345,000 barrels a day.
places.more: Promoters bused would-be investors to the oil field, served them a free lunch in circus tents, and told stories of fortunes made in oil. In 1923 the state limited how much stock could be sold in a well. By 1938 the field had produced more than 440 million barrels. In 1962 Carroll Shelby set up shop in Dean Moon's speed shop here. He had AC Cars of England ship him lightweight roadsters with no engines, fitted them with a 260-cubic-inch V8, and the Shelby Cobra was born.

places.name: San Gabriel River and Rio Hondo
places.text: The freeway crosses the San Gabriel River here, beside the 605 junction, and the Rio Hondo, Spanish for deep river, about two and a half miles to the northwest. The two run about two miles apart and were once one restless system. Before levees, the San Gabriel jumped between outlets with winter storms, and after a flood in the late 1860s it cut a new course, leaving its old bed to become the Rio Hondo.
places.more: On January 8, 1847, during the Mexican-American War, American troops won the Battle of Río San Gabriel on the west bank of what is now the Rio Hondo, near Washington Boulevard, because the San Gabriel flowed there then. The river is named for Mission San Gabriel, founded beside it in 1771, and at least 26 Tongva villages stood along it. It once had the largest steelhead runs in Southern California. After big floods in 1914, 1934 and 1938, the rivers were dammed and lined, and spreading grounds now soak storm water into the ground. About a third of the water used in southeast Los Angeles County comes from the San Gabriel.
places.spot: Look for a wide river channel passing under the freeway beside the 605 junction.

places.name: Downey, Apollo and McDonald's
places.text: Downey, southwest of the freeway, is named for John Gately Downey, the youngest governor California ever had. Its big aircraft plant, run by North American Aviation, built all of the Apollo command and service modules, nine of which carried astronauts to the Moon. Less than a mile down Lakewood Boulevard stands the oldest McDonald's, a walk-up stand from 1953 that still has its original golden arches, two tall arches of sheet metal.
places.more: By 1941 the plant, then run by Vultee, was building 15 percent of America's military planes, and Vultee was the first aircraft company to build planes on a powered assembly line. The Space Shuttle was conceived there too, and the plant closed in 1999 after 70 years. Part of the site is now the Columbia Memorial Space Center, with BP-12, the first Apollo capsule to fly, out front. The McDonald's was only the second restaurant franchised by Richard and Maurice McDonald, before Ray Kroc came along, so it never had to modernize. In 1959 it got a custom sign of Speedee, a hamburger-headed chef who was McDonald's mascot before Ronald McDonald. After the 1994 Northridge earthquake the company closed it and planned to tear it down, but the Downey City Council stopped the demolition, and it reopened in 1996.

places.name: The Citadel
places.text: That long wall decorated like an ancient palace was built in 1929 as the Samson Tire and Rubber Company factory. Its architects modeled it on the castle of the Assyrian king Sargon II, in a style called Exotic Revival, and the same firm designed the Mayan Theater in Los Angeles. Tires were made here until 1978, and the old factory front is now the face of the Citadel Outlets.
places.more: This was ranch land, and its turn toward industry began in 1887, when the Santa Fe Railway built its main line through. After the tire plant closed, the city of Commerce bought the site in 1983 and had it redeveloped into an outlet center with a hotel beside it. Commerce itself became a city in 1960, to keep neighbors from annexing its industrial land. Taxes from the Citadel and from the Commerce Casino, a card club, help pay for libraries and other city services, and Commerce is one of the few California cities with free city buses. A light-rail station is planned here, set to open in 2035.
places.spot: Look for a long wall that looks like an ancient palace, beside the freeway.

places.name: The Sears tower
places.text: The tall Art Deco tower near the interchange belongs to the old Sears, Roebuck mail-order building, finished in 1927 in just 171 days. Its nine stories held about 11 acres of floor space, shipping catalog orders to the Rocky Mountain and Pacific Coast states. Over the years its 226-foot tower and Sears sign were called a beacon for Eastsiders returning home on the freeways.
places.more: Inside, workers filled orders on roller skates, gliding through the aisles and dropping items onto corkscrew slides that carried them down to waiting trucks and trains. More than 100,000 people came to see it in its first month. The mail-order center closed in 1992, ending jobs for 585 full-time and 775 part-time workers, and the ground-floor store closed in 2021 after nearly 94 years. Boxer Oscar De La Hoya, a Boyle Heights native who shopped there as a child with his mother, tried twice to buy and revive the building. Plans for its future have come and gone since the 1990s.
places.spot: Look for a tall Art Deco tower rising above a huge old building.
places.wiki: Sears, Roebuck & Company Mail Order Building (Los Angeles, California)

places.name: East Los Angeles Interchange
places.text: This tangle of ramps is the East Los Angeles Interchange, where Interstate 5, Interstate 10, U.S. 101 and State Route 60 meet on 135 acres of Boyle Heights. A 2008 count put more than 550,000 vehicles a day through its southern part, and it is often called the busiest freeway interchange in the world. Radio traffic reporter Bill Keene called it Malfunction Junction.
places.more: Construction began in 1961, with 32 bridges, 20 walls and a $17,000 model to plan the ramps. It is officially the Eugene A. Obregon Memorial Interchange, honoring a Marine who received the Medal of Honor. This part of Interstate 5, the Golden State Freeway, was proposed in 1953, and Eastside residents fought it because it would cut through and wipe out large parts of Boyle Heights. Councilman Edward Roybal chaired a committee to block or reroute it, but it was built anyway. Boyle Heights takes its name from Andrew Boyle, an Irishman who bought 22 acres on the bluffs above the river and grew grapes there in the 1860s.
places.spot: Count how many ramps and bridges you can see stacked up at once.

places.name: Yaanga and the Tongva
places.text: Across the river, where downtown Los Angeles now stands, was Yaanga, recorded as the largest and most influential Tongva village in the region. At its center grew a great sycamore later called El Aliso, a landmark known to traders from as far away as present-day Yuma. The Portolá expedition reached Yaanga in 1769, and in 1781 Spanish settlers founded the pueblo of Los Angeles next to it.
places.more: The Tongva homeland, Tovaangar, covers about 4,000 square miles of the Los Angeles Basin and the southern Channel Islands. The people of Yaanga were forced to labor for the missions and to build the new town, and settlers moved their village again and again. In 1845 the last land set aside for them was sold for 200 dollars and they were pushed across the river into what is now Boyle Heights, and in 1847 that site was razed, reportedly with the city council's approval. Traces of Yaanga have turned up around Union Station and the old Plaza. In 1994 California recognized the Gabrieleño, or Tongva, as the aboriginal tribe of the Los Angeles Basin, though no Tongva group has federal recognition.

places.name: Arroyo Seco Parkway
places.text: The freeway crosses the Los Angeles River here, where the Arroyo Seco flows in, and meets the Arroyo Seco Parkway, one of the oldest freeways in the United States. It was dedicated on December 30, 1940, and opened the next day, in time for crowds heading to the Rose Parade and Rose Bowl in Pasadena. It was the first road built under a 1939 California law that let the state limit access to a few set points.
places.more: Arroyo Seco is Spanish for dry creek, a seasonal stream that runs from the San Gabriel Mountains through Pasadena, and the parkway follows it. Because the land made overpasses easy, the whole parkway cost $5.75 million, under $1 million a mile. Its tight curves and short ramps, with no room to speed up, have barely changed, and its crash rate is about twice that of other freeways. One side of the parkway runs through four Art Deco tunnels in Elysian Park, built for Figueroa Street between 1931 and 1936. The parkway is a National Scenic Byway and a National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark.
places.spot: Look for green signs pointing to Pasadena and the Arroyo Seco Parkway.

places.name: Elysian Park and Chavez Ravine
places.text: The wooded hills beside the freeway are Elysian Park, created in 1886 and, at 600 acres, one of the largest parks in Los Angeles. Tucked into them is Chavez Ravine, home of Dodger Stadium. By the 1940s the ravine held three close-knit, mostly Mexican American neighborhoods, La Loma, Palo Verde and Bishop, where many families lived because of housing discrimination elsewhere in the city.
places.more: In the early 1950s the city bought or condemned their homes for a public housing project called Elysian Park Heights, with two dozen 13-story towers. Then a new mayor called public housing un-American, and the project was dropped. In 1958 voters approved a deal trading 352 acres of the ravine to the Dodgers, and the last holdouts lost a ten-year struggle known as the Battle of Chavez Ravine. Dodger Stadium opened in 1962. At the foot of these hills by the river, the founders of Los Angeles dug their first water system in 1781, an earthen ditch called the Zanja Madre, or Mother Trench. A brick piece of it survives beside the light-rail tracks at Los Angeles State Historic Park, an old rail yard nicknamed the Cornfield, where so many newcomers first stepped off the train that it is called the Ellis Island of Los Angeles.
places.spot: Look for tree-covered hills rising close beside the freeway.

zones.label: San Onofre and San Clemente
zones.text: The freeway runs above San Onofre's beaches and the surf breaks of Trestles at the north edge of Camp Pendleton. The Orange County line is at Cristianitos Road, beside the hillside streets of Spanish-style San Clemente.

seasons.winter: Winter storms can push San Mateo Creek through the sandbar at its mouth, letting steelhead trout swim upstream to spawn.
seasons.spring: After heavy rains, a small seasonal stream usually runs through Trestles in winter and spring.

zones.label: Dana Point and Capistrano Valley
zones.text: Between Dana Point and Mission Viejo the freeway runs inland through the valley of San Juan and Trabuco creeks, Acjachemen homeland, past the mission town of San Juan Capistrano, with the ranch lands of Rancho Mission Viejo to the east.

seasons.winter: Almost all of the area's roughly 12 inches of yearly rain falls between November and March.
seasons.spring: The mission's cliff swallows traditionally return around March 19, Saint Joseph's Day.
seasons.fall: Tradition says the swallows leave around October 23, the old feast day of Saint John of Capistrano.

zones.label: Saddleback Valley
zones.text: Suburbs of Mission Viejo, Laguna Hills and Lake Forest fill the Saddleback Valley below the mountain's two peaks, and Interstate 405 meets this freeway at the El Toro Y.

seasons.winter: During most winters, snow dusts Santiago Peak, the higher summit of Saddleback, at least once.
seasons.fall: Autumn is the season known for hot, dry Santa Ana winds, which create critical fire weather in the hills.

zones.label: Irvine Ranch and Tustin
zones.text: Flat land that was the Irvine Ranch's lima bean fields and citrus groves is now Irvine's planned villages and Tustin's old Marine base, where one giant blimp hangar still stands.

seasons.summer: Late spring and early summer bring June Gloom, with overcast mornings and occasional drizzle.

zones.label: Santa Ana and Anaheim
zones.text: The freeway crosses the Santa Ana River and the Orange Crush interchange and passes Christ Cathedral and Disneyland, on a plain that was vineyards in the 1800s and orange groves into the 1950s.

seasons.winter: The Santa Ana River carries only a small flow except in the brief winter rainy season, when it is prone to flash floods.
seasons.fall: Santa Ana winds bring hot, dry autumn weather, and their wind damage is most common along the Santa Ana River basin.

zones.label: Buena Park to Norwalk
zones.text: Between Buena Park and Downey the freeway crosses the line between Orange and Los Angeles counties and runs through the Gateway Cities of La Mirada, Santa Fe Springs and Norwalk, on Rancho Los Nietos land that later held olive groves, dairies and oil fields.

zones.label: Downey, Commerce and East LA
zones.text: The freeway crosses the San Gabriel River and the Rio Hondo and runs through aerospace Downey, the rail-side factories of Commerce, and East Los Angeles.

zones.label: Boyle Heights to Elysian Park
zones.text: The freeway threads the East Los Angeles Interchange in Boyle Heights, runs through Lincoln Heights, the city's first suburb, and crosses the Los Angeles River where the Arroyo Seco joins it, beside the wooded hills of Elysian Park.

trivia.q: San Onofre is Spanish for Saint Onuphrius. Who was he?
trivia.why: The area was named for Saint Onuphrius, a hermit from fourth-century Egypt.

trivia.q: What is the famous surf spot Trestles named after?
trivia.why: Surfers named it for the wooden railroad trestle over San Mateo Creek that they walked under to reach the beach.

trivia.q: Where do the swallows of Capistrano spend the winter?
trivia.why: The cliff swallows winter around Goya, Argentina, and fly about 6,000 miles north each spring.

trivia.q: Trabuco Creek is named for something a Portolá expedition soldier lost in 1769. What was it?
trivia.why: Trabuco is Spanish for blunderbuss, a kind of old shotgun, and the gun was never found.

trivia.q: El Toro, the old name of Lake Forest, means what in Spanish?
trivia.why: El Toro means the bull; the town became the city of Lake Forest in 1991.

trivia.q: Jamboree Road is named for what 1953 event?
trivia.why: The 1953 National Scout Jamboree was held on Irvine Ranch land, and the road that served it was renamed Jamboree Road.

trivia.q: What were Tustin's giant wooden hangars built to hold during World War II?
trivia.why: The Navy built them for blimps that patrolled the coast in World War II.

trivia.q: About how many panes of glass cover the Crystal Cathedral, now Christ Cathedral?
trivia.why: The building has 10,000 rectangular panes, mirrored outside and see-through inside.

trivia.q: The name Anaheim joins Ana, for the Santa Ana River, with a German word meaning what?
trivia.why: The German founders named it Annaheim, home by the Santa Ana River.

trivia.q: When Cordelia Knott began serving fried chicken in June 1934, how many dinners did she serve?
trivia.why: She served eight fried chicken dinners at 65 cents each; today the restaurant serves more than 1.5 million a year.

trivia.q: Who is the mascot on the 1959 sign at the oldest McDonald's, in Downey?
trivia.why: Speedee, a little hamburger-headed chef, was McDonald's mascot before Ronald McDonald.

trivia.q: How did workers fill orders in the giant Sears mail-order building in Boyle Heights?
trivia.why: Workers roller-skated around the building and sent items down corkscrew slides to trucks and trains.
